Give separate forecasts the dependence of a joint model

Source: R/model-coupled.R
coupled.Rd

coupled() wraps a model (the base model) and a joint model (the template): its forecasts keep the margins of the base model and take the dependence between ages, years and strata from the template, by ensemble copula coupling (ECC; Schefzik, Thorarinsdottir and Gneiting 2013). mt_couple() does the same with two sets of forecast draws. Status: published (the ECC-R variant), with the package-specific choices listed below; section and equation numbers refer to the paper.

Usage

coupled(spec, template)

mt_couple(draws, template, seed = NULL)

Arguments

spec

The base model specification (margins).

template

For coupled(), a model specification whose draws give the dependence, usually a joint model of the same strata; for mt_couple(), its forecast draws (mt_draws).

draws

Forecast draws (mt_draws) that give the margins.

seed

Random seed for the ranks of tied template values (NULL leaves the random number generator as it is).

Value

coupled(): a model specification; its fit holds the fit of the template in $coupling$template, and its forecasts report the coupling in $coupling (template, number of margins and share of margins with tied template values). mt_couple(): the draws with the values of each margin reordered, and the coupling in $coupling.

Details

Method (Sections 4.1 and 4.2). Both models are fitted to the same data and forecast with the same number of draws M. A margin is one cell of the forecast: an age, a forecast year and a stratum. For each margin, the M values of the base model are sorted, and draw m receives the value whose rank among them equals the rank of draw m of the template among the template's values (eq. 4.3). Each margin keeps exactly the values of the base model. The draws take the multivariate rank structure (the empirical copula) of the template, and so its Spearman rank correlation between any two margins. The margins of the paper are weather variables at locations and lead times; here they are the cells of the grid, so the template sets the dependence between strata, between ages and between years. The template's draws must be exchangeable (Section 4); draws of a fitted model are.

Variant (Section 4.3). The base model's draws are a random sample from its forecast distribution of each margin, so the method is ECC-R, with the sample taken by the base model's simulation. The paper recommends ECC-Q, which uses the equidistant quantiles F^-1(m / (M + 1)) of each margin and did better in its case study (Section 5.3); it needs the quantile function of each margin, which models that forecast by simulation do not give.

Ties. Template values that are tied within a margin get their ranks at random, as the paper suggests (Section 4.1, footnote 6), with the random number generator of the forecast (seed). Tied base values need nothing, since only their sorted values are used. Draws of expected rates seldom have ties; predictive draws often have them, since deaths are counts. Margins without template draws (a stratum where the template failed) keep the order of the base model, with a warning.

Package-specific choices.

  • coupled() couples the draws of the models before observation noise: for models of expected rates (such as lee_carter() and cae()) the expected rates. Predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) then add the base model's Poisson (or negative binomial) deaths given the coupled rates, independent across cells, as for every model of the package. Without noise the margins are those of the base model exactly; with noise they are the same in distribution. The paper applies the ranks to the forecast of the observed quantity itself.

  • Around a reconciled base model (coupled(reconciled(...), ...)), the bottom strata are coupled and the aggregates recomputed, so the draws stay coherent. Coupling before reconciling, reconciled(spec, hierarchy, dependence = "ecc", template = ), is the order that gives the totals the template's dependence between the parts.

What changes. Coupling changes no single cell: the forecast distribution of each cell is that of the base model, so scores of single cells, such as their CRPS or the coverage of their intervals, change only by simulation noise. It changes quantities computed from several cells: totals over strata, gaps between strata, life expectancy (over ages) and cumulative changes (over years). The template should be a joint model (li_lee(), cae(), coherent_fdm(), tucker3(), coda(coherent = TRUE)); a template fitted per stratum has independent strata and gives a warning (class mt_warning_coupled).

The Schaake shuffle (Clark et al. 2004) reorders draws in the same way by the ranks of past observations; ECC takes the ranks from a model's forecast of the same years (Schefzik et al. 2013, Section 3.4). reconciled(dependence = "schaake") and mt_reconcile(dependence = "schaake") apply the Schaake shuffle with the observed changes of distinct training years; dependence = "empirical" applies it to the whole paths of each stratum, which keeps the dependence between the ages and years of each stratum.

mt_couple() couples two sets of draws with the same ages, years, strata and number of draws. Both should describe the same quantity (both predictive or both not). Couple before reconciling: draws reconciled before give a warning, because each stratum is reordered separately and their totals no longer add up.

References

Schefzik R, Thorarinsdottir TL, Gneiting T (2013). Uncertainty quantification in complex simulation models using ensemble copula coupling. Statistical Science 28(4): 616-640. doi:10.1214/13-STS443

Clark M, Gangopadhyay S, Hay L, Rajagopalan B, Wilby R (2004). The Schaake shuffle: a method for reconstructing space-time variability in forecasted precipitation and temperature fields. Journal of Hydrometeorology 5(1): 243-262.

See also

cae(), li_lee(); reconciled() with dependence = "ecc".

Examples

x <- mt_subset(mt_example_regions(years = 2000:2019, regions = 2), ages = c(60, Inf))
fit <- mt_fit(coupled(lee_carter(), template = cae()), x)
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 5, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
fc$coupling
#> $template
#> [1] "CAE (order 1)"
#> 
#> $method
#> [1] "ECC-R"
#> 
#> $margins
#> [1] 700
#> 
#> $tied
#> [1] 0
#> 
# the same with draws
fc_lc <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(), x), h = 5, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
fc_cae <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(cae(), x), h = 5, n_draws = 100, seed = 2)
fc2 <- mt_couple(fc_lc, fc_cae, seed = 3)
